items.body_md:
Today, five documents — Dkts. 194 through 198 — landed on the Poolin docket, all filed September 2, with no publicly available metadata describing their content or filer. Until those pleadings are pulled from CM/ECF or __[Verita Global](https://veritaglobal.net/poolin)__, their classification cannot be confirmed; any creditor tracking recovery exposure should retrieve them directly before the September 8 bid deadline. Dkt. 191 (August 31) is a BNC Certificate of Notice, filing infrastructure only.

The substantive development that now demands attention is a creditor's pending motion to appoint a Chapter 11 trustee, set for hearing on October 21, 2026. 
Poolin Technology is in the opening phase of a Chapter 11 wind-down centered on selling substantially all of the debtors' assets and pursuing a liquidating plan; a creditor's motion to appoint a Chapter 11 trustee is set for October 21, 2026.
 That motion is substantive and important on both axes: trustee appointment would strip existing management of debtor-in-possession control, displace the CRO, and hand the sale process and estate administration to a court-appointed fiduciary. 
All three entities remain debtors in possession, meaning existing management continues to run day-to-day affairs under court oversight rather than handing control to an outside trustee.
 A successful trustee motion would end that posture entirely — affecting who controls the § 363 sale, negotiates the Rule 9019 compromise at Dkt. 190, and ultimately makes distributions. For wallet-holder creditors owed 
$163,723,500 in unsecured wallet-holder IOUs
 against a 
$52 million stalking-horse covering the Tarbush ($37 million) and Pyote ($15 million) West Texas sites — roughly 32 cents on the dollar against the IOU pool before administrative costs and priority claims
 — who controls the estate matters as much as what the auction produces.

The October 21 trustee hearing sits well after the immediate sale milestones, but its shadow falls on every stage between now and confirmation of any liquidating plan. The Rule 9019 compromise at Dkt. 190 (filed August 28) remains unresolved; its counterparty, subject matter, and dollar amount are not disclosed in the public docket metadata, and the objection deadline — running approximately 21 days from the August 28 filing — expires around September 18, the same date as the sale hearing before Judge O'Hagan. Pachulski Stang Ziehl & Jones LLP's retention as committee counsel (Dkt. 179, filed August 24, objection deadline August 31) should now be effective absent a timely objection, giving the Official Committee of Unsecured Creditors a well-resourced litigation presence at precisely the moment the trustee motion, the 9019 settlement, and the sale hearing converge. The next hard deadline is September 8 — 
qualified bids for the debtors' assets are due by September 8, 2026, with an auction scheduled for September 10, 2026, if competing bids are received.

items.body_md:
On August 31, the Bankruptcy Notification Center docketed Dkt. 191, a certificate of notice tied to an order — filing infrastructure, not a substantive event. The only docket entry with analytical weight in the current window is Dkt. 190 (filed August 28), a motion to approve a compromise under Rule 9019. A Rule 9019 motion is substantive: it seeks court authorization for a settlement of some claim, dispute, or controversy affecting the estate, and if approved it will bind creditors to whatever terms the estate negotiated. The docket metadata does not identify the counterparty, the subject matter, or the dollar amount; the underlying pleading must be pulled directly from CM/ECF or __[Verita Global](https://veritaglobal.net/poolin)__ to assess materiality to recovery. Under the District of New Jersey's standard practice, a Rule 9019 motion carries a 21-day objection period running from the filing date, placing the objection deadline at approximately September 18 — the same date as the sale hearing before Judge O'Hagan. That overlap is operationally significant: any creditor or party in interest contesting the settlement terms must act on a compressed timeline coinciding with the most consequential hearing on the docket.

The qualified bid deadline arrives one week from today, September 8. Competing bids received by that date trigger the West Texas mining asset auction on September 10 at 10:00 a.m. Eastern at Archer & Greiner's offices in Voorhees, New Jersey (or virtually, or at another debtors-designated location). If no qualified bids clear the stalking-horse floor, the September 10 auction is a formality and Thor CALAP LLC acquires the Pyote and Tarbush sites on its existing $52 million terms. Sale objections are due September 16 at 5:00 p.m. Eastern; the sale hearing before Judge O'Hagan follows on September 18 at 11:00 a.m.

The next concrete milestone is September 8 — the qualified bid deadline — which will determine whether the auction is competitive or a single-bidder formality. The Rule 9019 compromise at Dkt. 190 warrants immediate attention from any creditor tracking recovery exposure; until the underlying motion is reviewed, its impact on estate value or claim treatment cannot be assessed.

items.body_md:
Today, the nonbinding indications of interest deadline expires
 — the first hard gate in the sale process since Judge O'Hagan entered the bidding procedures order on August 17. 
Prospective buyers seeking any portion of the assets had until today to submit nonbinding expressions of interest, with binding qualified bids due September 8.
 The IOI submissions are not filed on the docket and their contents will not be publicly disclosed; what the estate's investment banker receives today will determine whether the September 10 auction is competitive or a formality ceding the assets to stalking-horse Thor CALAP LLC at the floor. 
The prepetition marketing process generated 28 NDAs, seven LOIs, and three additional indications of interest
 before the petition date, so some market interest pre-existed — but 
NDAs and indications of interest fall short of qualified offers, and prospective buyers still have to value these particular sites above the Thor CALAP terms after accounting for development needs, contracts, and closing risk.


On the docket, Dkts. 180–183 (filed August 26) and the unnumbered hearing-rescheduled entry (filed August 27) each carry generic labels — "Document," "Document," "Motion (Generic)," "Document," and "Hearing Rescheduled" — without descriptive text available in public-facing records. The motion at Dkt. 181 is the only filing that could be substantive; without confirmed document text it cannot be classified with precision, and it is noted here as unverified pending the underlying pleading's public availability. The hearing-rescheduled entry is procedurally important to the extent it affects a near-term date, but the affected hearing and its new date are not identifiable from docket metadata alone. Dkts. 185 and 186 are BNC certificates of notice and carry no independent weight. Anyone tracking a specific motion or hearing in this case should pull the underlying documents directly from the court's CM/ECF system or __[Verita Global](https://veritaglobal.net/poolin)__ to confirm the affected event.


Creditors meet remotely tomorrow, August 28, at 9:00 a.m. ET for the Section 341 examination, where they can question company representatives under oath.
 That examination is the next concrete milestone and carries real weight for recovery analysis: it is the first opportunity for the creditor body — including the ~11,700 wallet IOU holders — to question CRO Michael DuFrayne on record regarding the pre-petition fund movements underlying the Chapter 11 trustee motion (Dkt. 103). The qualified bid deadline follows on September 8, 
with the auction set for September 10 at 10:00 a.m. Eastern, at Archer & Greiner's offices in Voorhees, New Jersey, virtually, or at another location designated by the debtors.
 
Sale objections are due September 16 at 5:00 p.m. Eastern, and the sale hearing before Judge O'Hagan is scheduled for September 18 at 11:00 a.m.

On August 24, Poolin's docket recorded one pro hac vice admission (Dkt. 176) and eight BNC certificates of notice (Dkts. 163–171) — all procedural-and-routine, with no bearing on recovery or timing. The master service list update filed by KCC dba Verita Global on August 21 (Dkt. 163) is likewise administrative. The open questions flagged in Friday's briefing — the content of Dkts. 155–162 and the disposition of the Elektron Energy Rule 9019 settlement following the August 20 hearing — remain unresolved on the face of the publicly available docket and require direct CM/ECF review to close out.

Over the weekend, broader press coverage crystallized the scale of the creditor exposure. 
Poolin's bankruptcy filing lists assets of between $1 million and $10 million against liabilities of as much as $500 million.
 
The petition estimates between 10,001 and 25,000 creditors.
 
Poolin told the court it entered Chapter 11 to carry out a sale of its business and preserve value for creditors, with qualified bids due by September 8 and an auction scheduled for September 10.
 That framing does nothing to close the asset-liability gap: 
Poolin filed Chapter 11 with $163.7 million in wallet IOUs owed to roughly 11,700 users with balances above $100, while the $52 million in signed stalking-horse offers covers Texas mining assets — not wallet cash — and equals just 31.8% of those IOUs before costs.
 The structural disconnect between what the sale covers and where the bulk of creditor claims sit remains the central recovery question.

The next concrete milestone is Thursday, August 27 — the nonbinding indications of interest deadline — followed immediately by the Section 341 creditors' meeting on August 28 (remote). 
Creditors are scheduled to meet remotely on August 28 at 9 a.m. ET, a standard step where creditors can question company representatives under oath.
 The Section 341 examination is the first formal opportunity for the creditor body — including the wallet IOU holders — to probe CRO Michael DuFrayne on the pre-petition fund movements that underlie the pending trustee motion (Dkt. 103). The qualified bid deadline follows on September 8, and the auction on September 10, assuming at least one competing bid clears the qualification threshold.

items.body_md:
Today, the Poolin Technology docket recorded eight motions — Dkts. 155 through 162 — all filed on August 21 and classified in the court's system as "Motion (Generic)." The docket metadata provides no further description of their subject matter, and no secondary reporting has identified their content as of this writing; they cannot be characterized with precision and will require direct review of the filed documents to assess materiality. Eight simultaneous generic motion filings in a single day is unusual in this case and warrants monitoring: depending on their content, they could represent anything from omnibus claim objections to contract rejection motions to creditor-initiated relief requests — all of which would be substantive. Confirmation will require access to the underlying documents on the CM/ECF docket for Case No. 26-18325 (Bankr. D.N.J., Judge O'Hagan).

The August 20 hearing on the Rule 9019 settlement motion (Dkt. 129) — the Elektron Energy settlement scheduled for 11:00 a.m. in Courtroom 2, Trenton, per the order shortening time (Dkt. 137) — has produced no confirming docket entry as of today. The docket reflects a "Hearing Held" entry for August 20, which is consistent with the hearing having proceeded, but no resulting order has appeared. Until an order issues, the Elektron Energy liability — 
a $1,344,788.13 balance owed to Lonestar Dream for the March 2025 to March 2026 period, held in escrow pending release conditions
 — remains unresolved in terms of whether it closes out as a settlement, survives as a cure amount disclosed in Dkt. 149, or persists as a general unsecured claim. That ambiguity has direct bearing on what travels clean to the buyer at closing.


August 21 was the deadline for the assumption and assignment notice, with the assigned contracts schedule and proposed cure amounts
 — executed by Dkt. 149, filed August 19. 
August 27 is the deadline for nonbinding indications of interest
, the next immediate milestone in the sale timeline, followed by 
the September 8 qualified bid deadline, the September 10 auction, and the September 16 sale hearing.
 Counterparties to executory contracts and unexpired leases now hold cure objection rights running from service of Dkt. 149; silence operates as consent to the stated cure amounts, and any undisclosed dispute can encumber title post-closing. The trustee motion (Dkt. 103, hearing October 21) remains pending and unchanged; if granted before the September 16 sale hearing, CRO Michael DuFrayne's authority terminates and an independent trustee assumes control of the auction process. Dkts. 150–154 are BNC certificates of notice — not reported. The immediate priority is identifying the content of Dkts. 155–162 and obtaining the order, if any, that emerged from the August 20 Elektron Energy hearing.

items.body_md:
On August 19, Poolin Technology filed the Notice of Sale by Auction and Sale Hearing (Dkt. 148) and the Notice of Cure Amount and Potential Assumption and Assignment of Executory Contracts and Unexpired Leases (Dkt. 149), both issued pursuant to Dkt. 138 — Judge O'Hagan's August 17 order approving bidding procedures for the sale of substantially all of the debtor's assets. Together, these two filings execute the auction machinery the court authorized three days earlier: Dkt. 148 formally notifies the market of the auction date and the sale hearing, while Dkt. 149 discloses the cure amounts attached to any executory contracts or unexpired leases the estate proposes to assume and assign to a buyer. The cure notice is the first document in this case to put counterparties on the clock: 
the assumption and assignment notice, with the assigned contracts schedule and proposed cure amounts, was due August 21, 2026
 — meaning objections to cure amounts and to assumption or assignment will run from that notice's service date. Any counterparty that disputes a cure figure must object before the sale hearing; silence operates as consent to the stated amount, and an undisclosed cure dispute can encumber title post-closing.

For creditor recovery, the cure notice carries direct financial relevance. The estate's first-day declaration disclosed an outstanding balance of $1,344,788.13 owed to Elektron Energy in connection with the Texas power agreements; whether that figure appears as a proposed cure amount — or is instead the subject of the pending Rule 9019 settlement motion (Dkt. 129) — determines whether it travels with the assets to the buyer or settles separately before closing. That ambiguity remains open: the 9019 settlement (Dkt. 129) was filed August 14 on shortened time (Dkt. 137, order to shorten entered August 17, scheduling a hearing for August 20 at 11:00 a.m.), and no docket entry yet confirms the outcome of that hearing. If the 9019 hearing proceeded today as scheduled, a resulting order will be the next substantive filing to watch; its content — whether it resolves the Elektron Energy dispute and on what terms — determines whether that liability survives as a cure amount, a claim against the estate, or neither. 
Judge O'Hagan cleared Poolin Technology to pursue the asset sale at the August 14 hearing, also giving stalking-horse Thor CALAP LLC time to evaluate a neighboring property for an AI data center in Texas.
 
The qualified bid deadline is September 8, 2026, with the auction scheduled for September 10 and the sale hearing set for September 16.


On the trustee motion front, creditor Lin Liang filed an amended notice of hearing (Dkt. 143) on August 18, conforming the hearing date on her motion to appoint a Chapter 11 trustee (Dkt. 103) to the October 21, 2026 date Judge O'Hagan set by text order on August 17 — no new substantive argument, just calendaring alignment. The trustee motion remains pending and unresolved; if granted before the sale hearing on September 16, the CRO's authority terminates and an independent trustee assumes control of the sale process, which would at minimum create timing risk for the auction. 
The creditor moved for appointment of a Chapter 11 trustee, alleging the company's principal absconded from China to the U.S. with customer funds.
 Archer & Greiner's amended July fee statement (Dkt. 146, correcting Dkt. 145, objection deadline September 2) is procedural and routine. Dkts. 150–154 are BNC certificates of notice — filing infrastructure, not reported. The next concrete milestone is the September 8 qualified bid deadline for the West Texas auction, preceded by whatever order emerges from today's 9019 hearing if the August 20 at 11:00 a.m. hearing proceeded as scheduled.

items.body_md:
On August 18, an unnamed professional filed a monthly fee statement (Dkt. 145) and a support document (Dkt. 143), and August 17 produced the substantive cluster that warrants attention today: an amended motion combined with a retention application (Dkt. 140), a generic motion of unverified subject matter (Dkt. 139), and — carrying the most analytical weight — an interim order on a final hearing (Dkt. 138), entered alongside a new shorten-time motion (Dkt. 137) and confirmed by a Hearing Scheduled entry (Dkt. 142).

Yesterday's briefing flagged that Dkt. 138's subject matter remained unverified from the docket labels alone and that the most plausible candidates were the August 14 Rule 9019 settlement motion (Dkt. 129) and its companion shorten-time motion (Dkt. 130). That uncertainty has not resolved: no secondary reporting has confirmed which pending matter Dkt. 138 addresses, and the docket labels do not specify. What the August 17 cluster confirms structurally is that Judge O'Hagan is running at least one matter on an expedited, interim-then-final track, with a final hearing now calendared (Dkt. 142). If Dkt. 138 provides interim relief on the 9019 settlement, the content of that relief — whether it touches lien priority, claim allowance, or asset title on the Texas properties — is material to creditor recovery ahead of the September 8 qualified bid deadline. Dkt. 139, the generic motion, remains unverified as to subject matter; classify up until the document is accessible. Dkt. 140 mirrors the form of the August 14 amended retention motion (Dkt. 127); absent evidence of a contested objection, it is procedural and routine.

The trustee motion filed by creditor Lin Liang (Dkt. 103) continues to sit unresolved on the public record alongside the 9019 settlement (Dkt. 129). Both need resolution before the auction: the trustee motion, if granted, displaces the CRO entirely and changes the investigative posture of the estate; the 9019 settlement, if it touches the Elektron Energy billing dispute — which, per the first-day declaration, left a balance of $1,344,788.13 — determines whether that liability encumbers the Texas assets going into the sale. Dkts. 132–136 are BNC certificates of notice, and Dkt. 144 is a certificate of service — filing infrastructure, omitted. The next concrete milestone is September 8, the qualified bid deadline for the West Texas auction, followed by the September 10 auction for the Pyote and Tarbush sites.

items.body_md:
On August 14, Judge O'Hagan cleared Poolin Technology to proceed with the September asset sale and approved terms giving stalking-horse bidder Thor CALAP LLC additional time to pursue a neighboring Texas property for an AI data center — removing the most immediate structural threat to the sale timeline. 
The New Jersey bankruptcy court confirmed that Poolin Technology can pursue the planned next-month sale, with the judge granting Thor CALAP additional time in connection with its interest in adjacent land for AI data center development in Texas.
 The hearing on August 14 was the bidding-procedures hearing flagged in prior coverage as the sale's first critical gatekeeping event.

Dkt. 129, filed August 14, is a motion to approve a compromise or settlement under Rule 9019. The subject of that compromise is partially illuminated by Dkt. 118 — the Declaration of Michael DuFrayne filed August 13 in support of a "Stipulation and Agreed Order Resolving Objection to Bidding Procedures Motion," which itself relates to the Amended Motion (Dkt. 30). Read together, these entries show that at least one objection to the bidding procedures was resolved by stipulation before the August 14 hearing rather than litigated. The 9019 motion at Dkt. 129 is accompanied by a motion to shorten time (Dkt. 130), indicating the debtors are seeking accelerated briefing and hearing on the settlement — unsurprising given the September 8 qualified bid deadline. The terms and counterparties to the 9019 settlement are not disclosed in the docket descriptions; confirmation of the precise settlement terms requires the full filed document, which is not reproduced here. What the combination of Dkt. 129 and 130 does signal is that a contested matter the estate needed cleared before the auction — whether a bidding-procedures objection, a creditor dispute, or an ancillary claim — has been papered and is being put before the court on a compressed schedule.

Dkts. 125, 126, 127, and 128 are retention applications filed August 14, including an amended motion that doubles as a retention filing. These are procedural in the ordinary sense — professional retentions are standard bankruptcy infrastructure — but their timing, filed on the same day as the bidding-procedures hearing and the 9019 motion, is consistent with the estate standing up its full professional team now that the sale timeline is locked. The creditors' committee appointed August 12 (Dkt. 112) will have its own retention needs, and the amended retention at Dkt. 127 may reflect the committee formalizing its advisors. None of the retentions appear contested on the current record. The trustee fight — creditor Lin Liang's motion to appoint a Chapter 11 trustee (Dkt. 103), whose application to shorten time was twice denied (Dkts. 109, 110) — remains pending on the standard timeline; nothing on August 14 resolved or advanced it, and the bidding-procedures clearance confirms the court is not letting that fight impede the sale process. Dkts. 121 and 123 (pro hac vice appearances) and Dkt. 122 (notice of appearance) are procedural and routine. Dkt. 117 — the transcript of the July 27 first-day hearing — is administrative record-keeping. Dkts. 119 and 120 (BNC certificates) are filing infrastructure.

The next concrete milestone is September 8, the qualified bid deadline for the West Texas assets (Pyote and Tarbush), followed by the auction on September 10 if more than one qualified bid is received. The 9019 motion at Dkt. 129, on shortened time, will have its own hearing before then; that hearing date will be set by order on Dkt. 130 and is not yet publicly confirmed.

items.body_md:
On August 10, a creditor filed Dkt. 103 — a motion to appoint a Chapter 11 trustee in Bankr. D.N.J. Case No. 26-18325 — alleging that Zhibiao "Kevin" Pan, Poolin's principal and sole equity holder, 
absconded from China to the U.S. with customer funds.
 That motion is the sharpest development in the case to date. Trustee appointment under 11 U.S.C. § 1104 displaces existing management and shifts control of the estate to a court-supervised fiduciary; if granted, it would remove Pan — and, by extension, the debtor's current restructuring professionals acting at his direction — from any role in administering the sale process or the liquidating plan. The allegation of pre-petition fund transfers by the principal sits squarely within § 1104(a)(1) grounds (fraud, dishonesty, gross mismanagement), making this motion substantively weightier than a routine creditor complaint.

Dkt. 104 — a motion to shorten time — was filed the same day, almost certainly tied to the trustee motion, signaling the moving creditor is pressing for an expedited hearing rather than waiting for a standard briefing schedule. Dkt. 105 and Dkt. 106 are a response and an objection, respectively, filed on the same date; their precise targets cannot be confirmed from the docket metadata alone, but given the clustering with the trustee motion, they most likely address either the trustee motion or the shorten-time request, and may indicate that the debtor or another party moved immediately to oppose. The creditor's identity is not disclosed in the docket entry or in the paywalled __[Law360 article](https://www.law360.com/bankruptcy-authority/mid-cap/articles/2511097)__, which confirms the motion was filed but does not name the movant in its visible text.

The trustee motion lands at a structurally sensitive moment. The qualified-bid deadline for the West Texas auction (Pyote at $15 million; Tarbush at $37 million; combined floor $52 million from stalking-horse Thor CALAP LLC) is September 8, with the auction scheduled for September 10. 
The debtors — Poolin Technology, Lonestar Dream Inc., and Lonestar Taproot LLC — are all directly or indirectly owned by Pan.
 A trustee appointment before the auction would transfer control of bid evaluation, stalking-horse negotiations, and plan drafting to an independent fiduciary, with unknown consequences for deal timing and terms already in place. Even if the motion ultimately fails, the expedited posture (Dkt. 104) means Judge O'Hagan is likely to be asked to set a prompt hearing — one that may compete with, or run directly into, the September 8 bid deadline. The next concrete milestone is the court's ruling on the motion to shorten time, which will set the hearing date for the trustee motion and determine whether this fight resolves before or after qualified bids are due.

Dkts. 101–102 — two pro hac vice admissions — are omitted as procedural and routine.

On August 7, the clerk docketed the notice scheduling the § 341 meeting of creditors (Dkt. 97), setting the first formal opportunity for the U.S. Trustee and creditors to examine the debtors under oath. The § 341 meeting is procedural but carries timing significance: its scheduling confirms the case is moving on the standard Chapter 11 administrative track in parallel with the sale process, and any creditor — including wallet holders — may appear and pose questions directly to the debtors' representatives. The specific date and location are not established from available docket text; confirmation requires the docket entry itself.

Dkts. 98–100 — the objection, accompanying document, and exhibit filed on August 7 and 8 against the bidding procedures and sale motion — remain the substantive weight of the hearing set for Thursday, August 14 at 11 a.m. ET before Judge O'Hagan. The identity of the objecting party and the specific grounds are not established from available docket text. Thor CALAP LLC's no-cause diligence termination right expired by its contractual terms on August 9; no termination notice has appeared on the docket and no press outlet has reported exercise of that right, which is consistent with both the $15 million Pyote and $37 million Tarbush agreements remaining operative — but the debtors have not affirmatively represented that status on the record. A termination delivered directly to the debtors need not surface immediately as a court filing, so the stalking-horse status remains unverified until the August 14 hearing or an earlier affirmative representation by counsel.

The Notice of Docketing Error (filed August 7, no docket number assigned) is ministerial and carries no bearing on the substantive record. The next concrete milestone is the August 14 hearing at 11 a.m. ET: Judge O'Hagan's ruling on the bidding procedures and sale motion — including resolution of the Dkt. 98 objection — will determine whether the September 8 qualified-bid deadline, the September 10 auction, and the proposed September 16 sale hearing hold. For the 11,700 wallet holders carrying $163,723,500 in unsecured IOU claims, Thursday's ruling is the first judicial read on whether the sale framework survives intact.

The docket's movement since yesterday's briefing is thin but sequentially significant given where the case stands today. Dkt. 100, filed August 8 and logged as an Exhibit, is the only new entry since the close of the August 7 objection deadline. Its content is not confirmed from available docket text, but exhibit filings at this stage of a § 363 sale process typically attach supporting documentation to a pending motion — most likely supplementing the bidding-procedures and sale motion, or responding to Dkt. 98, the Objection filed August 7 — and should not be read as a substantive development absent confirmation of its subject matter. The filing's existence is noted; its weight cannot be assessed.

The more concrete event is one that falls outside the docket: Thor CALAP LLC's no-cause diligence exit right expires today, August 9. 
Thor CALAP LLC can terminate either deal over unsatisfactory diligence through August 9, five days before the court's scheduled hearing on the bidding process and sale.
 As of this briefing, no confirmed reporting or docket entry reflects an exercise of that right, and no termination notice has surfaced on the docket. That absence is not confirmation of waiver — Thor may transmit notice directly to the debtors without an immediate docket filing — and neither a press report nor a stipulation has appeared to confirm that the stalking horse remains in place. What confirmation would look like: a notice of termination filed on the docket, or, conversely, a statement by the debtors or a docket entry proceeding on the assumption that the purchase agreements remain operative. Until one or the other appears, the status of the stalking-horse commitment is unverified. The recovery posture for the 11,700 wallet holders carrying $163,723,500 in unsecured IOU claims hinges materially on this point: without a floor bid, the August 14 hearing would arrive with no approved procedures and no confirmed opening consideration.

The next confirmed milestone is the bid-procedures and sale hearing before Judge O'Hagan, which the docket shows was requested for August 14 at 11 a.m. ET — now approaching against a docket that carries at least one live objection (Dkt. 98) and an exhibit filing (Dkt. 100) whose relationship to that objection is unconfirmed. 
The proposed schedule beyond that hearing calls for a September 8 qualified-bid deadline, a September 10 auction, and a September 16 sale hearing.
 Whether Judge O'Hagan proceeds on August 14, adjourns, or takes the matter on a contested basis will be shaped by the content of Dkt. 98 and whether the debtors can represent that Thor's purchase agreements remain in effect. Both variables are unresolved as of today.

items.body_md:
Today's objection deadline has now closed — or closes by end of business — and the docket has delivered its most significant procedural development since the support cluster filed August 6: Dkt. 98, filed this morning, is logged as an Objection, the first contested filing against the bidding procedures and sale motion in *In re Poolin Technology PTE*, No. 26-18325 (Bankr. D.N.J., Judge O'Hagan). The identity of the objecting party and the precise grounds are not confirmed from docket text available to this briefing, but the filing's timing — the deadline itself — is consistent with a creditor, committee, or regulatory body preserving its objection rights for the August 14 hearing. Whether this is a targeted objection to a specific bid term, a broader challenge to the § 363 framework, or a cure-related filing cannot be stated with certainty at this stage; that content governs how the August 14 hearing is shaped and whether Judge O'Hagan proceeds, adjourns, or takes the matter on a contested basis.

Also filed this morning is Dkt. 97, logged as a Meeting of Creditors Chapter 11. 
Objections to the bidding procedures and sale motion were due August 7, and the court has scheduled a hearing for August 14 at 11 a.m. ET.
 The § 341 meeting entry is procedurally routine but confirms the case is tracking standard Chapter 11 administration in parallel with the sale process — it does not bear directly on recovery posture unless an examiner or U.S. Trustee observation surfaces anything adverse at that session. The undocketed Notice of Docketing Error, also filed August 7, has no confirmed substantive effect; such notices typically correct a filing deficiency rather than alter the underlying record. Against this backdrop, the six support filings from August 6 (Dkt. 89–94) now sit alongside a live objection: the procedural picture heading into August 14 is contested, not clean.

The objection's existence sharpens the stakes of the two concurrent pressures already in play. 
Thor may terminate through August 9 if, in its sole and absolute discretion, it finds diligence unsatisfactory, for any reason or no reason, leaving a no-cause exit three days before the requested bid-procedures hearing.
 A stalking-horse termination arriving simultaneously with a contested objection hearing would present Judge O'Hagan with a materially weakened sale framework: no floor bid, no approved procedures, and a contested § 363 record. 
Neither purchase agreement fixes how consideration divides between the two Lonestar estates — each leaves allocation to the buyer to be determined within 180 days after closing — and Poolin Technology is not a seller under either agreement.
 For the 11,700 wallet holders carrying $163,723,500 in unsecured IOU claims, that structural gap remains the central unresolved variable; 
the amount available to wallet creditors depends on estate-specific claims, any valid liens against net proceeds, transfer taxes, professional fees, other administrative costs, and the treatment of Poolin's intercompany claim.
 The next two milestones arrive in sequence: Thor's no-cause diligence exit right expires August 9, and the bid-procedures and sale hearing before Judge O'Hagan follows on August 14 at 11 a.m. ET — now against a docket that carries at least one live objection.
